title: Quantum-Inspired Probabilistic Resonance Theory for Neural Network Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to neural network optimization termed Probabilistic Resonance Theory (PRT), inspired by quantum mechanics. Traditional gradient descent methods often struggle with vanishing gradients, local minima, and slow convergence, particularly in complex, high-dimensional networks. PRT frames neural network training as a resonance phenomenon, mirroring the interaction of quantum systems. The core principle involves constructing a loss function that incorporates probabilistic resonance, drawing on concepts like superposition and interference. Specifically, the loss function is designed to encourage the network's weights to "resonate" at specific frequencies, effectively guiding the training process toward optimal configurations. Mathematical formulations detail the probabilistic resonance loss function (PRLF), the superposition weighting scheme (SWS), and the interference mitigation strategy (IMS). The theoretical framework demonstrates how these elements synergistically contribute to a more efficient and robust optimization process. Preliminary analysis suggests PRT's potential for significantly faster convergence and improved performance compared to conventional gradient descent methods, offering a new paradigm for neural network training.

title: GAN-Blot: A Controllable Structure-Style Synthesis Benchmark for Western Blot Forensics
abstract: Western blot (WB) images are widely used as key evidence in biomedical research. Recent scientific misconduct cases reveal that WB imagery is increasingly fabricated, making WB forensics a major concern for research integrity. However, while the progress of forensic detection techniques often relies on advances in forgery-generation techniques, the development of WB forensic techniques has been hindered by the lack of standardized appearance attribute definitions, image datasets, and controllable generation frameworks for WB imagery. To address this limitation, we present a controllable WB image synthesis framework, named GAN-Blot, for generating realistic synthetic WB images. We introduce a formulation that decomposes a WB image into a structure component and a style-reference component, enabling independent control over local protein-band geometry and the global visual appearance of a synthetic WB image. GAN-Blot integrates a dual-path autoencoding design with several style-alignment loss terms to enable implicit control over structure-style synthesis without predefined semantic appearance attributes. We further contribute a synthetic WB dataset containing more than 46K images and propose four evaluation protocols for controllable WB synthesis. Extensive experiments show that GAN-Blot can generate WB images with high fidelity in both protein-band structure and visual style. Under blind inspection, the generated images can fool domain experts and are not reliably distinguished from authentic WB images by existing detectors and screening platforms. These results demonstrate their utility as challenging controlled cases for validating and developing WB forensic methods.

title: Hierarchical Wasserstein Merging for Multi-Domain Multi-Task Learning: From Specialists to a Generalist
abstract: Multi-domain multi-task learning (MD-MTL) aims to build a single generalist model that performs well across heterogeneous domains and tasks. However, joint training often suffers from interference under distribution shifts. Existing model merging methods mostly operate on model parameters while overlooking the geometric structure of latent representation distributions across domains and tasks. To address these limitations, we propose Hierarchical Wasserstein Merging (HWM), a representation-level framework that models each domain-task specialist as a distribution of hidden representations on a shared support. HWM constructs task-level and global Wasserstein barycenters to capture within-task domain variation and cross-task structure, enabling either training-free specialist aggregation by Wasserstein-derived weights or training-based generalist learning through a hybrid Wasserstein alignment loss. Experiments on four NLP tasks across four domains per task show that HWM achieves superior effectiveness and generalization capability in MD-MTL settings.

title: Microtubule-Augmented Perceptron: Structured Biological Topology as an Inductive Bias for Reservoir Computing
abstract: Inspired by the intracellular structure of biological neurons, we propose a computational microtubule module that provides additional internal processing within a perceptron. We use a classical automata abstraction of the microtubule lattice geometry 13 protofilaments × 20 rings with a 3-monomer helical seam as a fixed reservoir substrate, training only a linear readout. This work uses purely classical dynamics; we explicitly exclude quantum or consciousness-related claims, as decoherence timescales make such mechanisms implausible in warm biological tissue. We evaluate whether the specific structure of the microtubule lattice provides any computational advantage over topologically matched alternatives. On a static parity task, the helical seam provides no measurable advantage over a seamless cylinder (Cliff's δ ≈ 0, p ≈ 1), while the lattice broadly outperforms random and dense topologies. On sequential MNIST where 784 pixels must be integrated one at a time the microtubule reservoir achieves 37.6% accuracy with 95% CI [36.9%, 38.4%] (25 seeds), outperforming a matched random reservoir (ESN, 23.3%, Cliff's δ = +1.0, p = 2.8 × 10⁻⁹) using only 11 trained readout parameters versus the ESN's 2,610 total parameters. A trained GRU achieves a higher mean (57.6%) but with 10× wider confidence intervals and 2,500× more trained parameters, and collapses to near-chance on some seeds due to vanishing gradients over 784 steps. Our results suggest that structured biological topology is most beneficial when temporal routing over long sequences is required, and provides no advantage for static classification tasks where the seam's orbital properties are irrelevant.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement: A Mathematical Model for Precise Simulation and Performance Prediction
abstract: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement explores the development of a novel mathematical model for simulating the evolution of quantum entanglement, offering a significant advancement over static models. This model leverages dynamic state evolution, providing a rigorous framework for predicting quantum computation's performance. The core mechanism centers around representing entanglement as a continuously evolving quantum state, driven by a dynamic set of rules. This approach allows for a more accurate and detailed simulation of entanglement dynamics, ultimately improving the prediction of quantum algorithm efficiency. This work presents a comprehensive theoretical foundation and initial implementation of this model, highlighting its potential for revolutionizing quantum computing research.

title: Title: Non-Local Quantum State Reconstruction via Entanglement Propagation
abstract: Quantum state reconstruction is a fundamental challenge in quantum information science, requiring the determination of a quantum system's initial state from measurement results. Traditional approaches often involve computationally intensive "offline" methods, limiting their applicability. This paper introduces a novel method for quantum state reconstruction utilizing entanglement propagation, offering a fundamentally different approach compared to existing techniques. We propose a quantum algorithm that iteratively propagates entanglement across a network, enabling the reconstruction of the initial state with enhanced efficiency. The core mechanism relies on the inherent properties of entanglement, allowing for a potentially faster and more robust reconstruction process. This research addresses the limitations of existing methods and presents a promising direction for future advancements in quantum state estimation.

title: Title: Adaptive Fractal Dimension Optimization in Machine Learning
abstract: This paper presents an innovative algorithm for adaptive fractal dimension optimization in machine learning, specifically targeting neural network layers. Traditional methods often rely on fixed fractal dimensions, limiting the model's flexibility. This work introduces a dynamic adaptation process, adjusting the fractal dimension during training to improve feature representation and mitigate overfitting. The core mechanism leverages a novel optimization strategy that continuously evaluates and refines the fractal dimension based on the data's complexity, offering a significant improvement over existing techniques. The proposed approach aims to unlock deeper feature representations and enhance model generalization performance.

title: Dynamic Particle Topological Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic particle topological optimization (DPTO) algorithm that leverages the dynamic behavior of particles within a topologically defined structure to optimize system parameters and achieve system stability. The algorithm utilizes a particle swarm optimization (PSO) approach with a modified topology, where particle positions and velocities are influenced by a dynamic force field. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in optimizing a complex system with multiple interacting components, showcasing improved stability compared to traditional optimization techniques. The core mechanism involves the continuous adjustment of the topology through particle interactions, ensuring a robust and adaptable optimization process. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's potential applications across various fields.

title: High-Order Matrix Gradient Propagation
abstract: High-order Matrix Gradient Propagation (H-HMP) presents a novel approach to gradient-based optimization, specifically designed to address the challenges of data distribution complexity and gradient stability. This paper introduces a new algorithm that dynamically adjusts the learning rate and gradient magnitude based on local data characteristics, aiming to enhance both training efficiency and model generalization. We detail the core mechanism of H-HMP, highlighting its adaptive parameter adjustment process and its ability to mitigate gradient vanishing and exploding. The algorithm's design incorporates a novel weighting scheme to refine the gradient based on local data variations, ultimately leading to improved convergence and performance compared to traditional gradient-based methods. This work presents a robust and adaptable framework for optimizing high-order matrices, offering a significant step towards more efficient and effective model training.

title: Zero-Divisor Cryptography A: Zero-Divisor Annihilation One-Way Function and Isotropic Subspace Steganographic Public-Key Encryption
abstract: This paper constructs two cryptographic primitives within the framework of the16-dimensional Cayley–Dickson algebra (Sedenion), whose hardness does not relyon cyclic groups or hidden subgroup structures. The first is a zero-divisor pathone-way function, whose security is based on the hardness of zero-divisor pathreconstruction: the public key is a nonzero element obtained by left-associativemultiplication of an anchor point by a sequence of zero-divisors; the private keyis the zero-divisor sequence itself. Recovering the private key from the public keyis equivalent to locating the unique non-collapsing sequence among exponentiallymany annihilating paths. Conventional discrete logarithm and Shor’s quantumalgorithm are not directly applicable under current knowledge. The second is anisotropic subspace steganographic public-key encryption, where the private key information is not stored in the linear components of the zero-divisor subspace, butencoded in the nonlinear associator remainder of boundary elements. If an adversary performs only linear projection, the information gain is strictly zero. Bothprotocols share the same underlying algebraic construction: an explicit zero-divisorsubspace basis of the 16-dimensional algebra over a finite field, a spectrum-guidedrigid core search algorithm, and a trilinear mapping characterization of boundaryassociators. The overall scheme uses the zero-divisor path one-way function asthe public-key anchoring and anti-forgery component, and the isotropic subspacesteganographic encryption as the semantically secure key encapsulation layer; theywork together to form a complete cryptographic system. Parameter analysis showsthat at the 128-bit security level, the public key size is about 4096 bits, and keygeneration, encryption, and decryption are all polynomial-time.

title: Title: Adaptive Geometric Model Parameter Adjustment via Graph Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive geometric model parameter adjustment method based on graph optimization, aiming to enhance the prediction accuracy of machine learning models. Traditional model parameter adjustments rely on predefined models, while this approach leverages the graph's inherent adaptability to achieve more effective parameter tuning. The core mechanism involves dynamically adjusting geometric model parameters based on graph structure, resulting in improved predictive performance. The research explores the effectiveness of this method through a series of experiments and demonstrates its ability to address limitations of conventional approaches. This work contributes to the field of machine learning through a novel graph-based optimization technique for model parameter adjustment.

title: Quantum Feature Multi-Scale Geometry Mapping
abstract: Quantum Feature Multi-Scale Geometry Mapping is a novel approach to quantum computing that leverages quantum feature extraction to dynamically map complex geometric structures onto quantum states. This method aims to enhance quantum computation efficiency by providing a more streamlined and automated process for mapping key geometric characteristics. Traditional geometric mapping techniques often rely on manual design, limiting scalability and adaptability. Our approach utilizes quantum feature extraction to establish a dynamic relationship between geometric descriptors and quantum states, thereby improving the efficiency of quantum computations. This research explores the potential of this methodology through theoretical analysis and preliminary implementations.

title: Algorithmic Complexity Reduction via Dynamic Parameter Tuning (ACPR)
abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Complexity Reduction via Dynamic Parameter Tuning (ACPR), a novel optimization technique designed to minimize computational complexity within complex systems. Traditional optimization methods often treat parameters in isolation, failing to account for their interconnected influence on overall system performance. ACPR employs a dynamically adjusted parameter learning strategy, continuously refining the system's parameters based on their impact on complexity, resulting in enhanced efficiency. This approach distinguishes itself through a holistic and adaptive optimization methodology, offering a substantial improvement over existing methods. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, training process, and performance evaluation, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing computational overhead across a range of benchmark datasets.

title: Field-Adaptive Generalized Functions (DSFT)
abstract: Field-Adaptive Generalized Functions (DSFT) is a novel approach to machine learning that leverages the power of generalized functions to dynamically adapt the representation of data within a model. This paper introduces a new algorithm, DFT, which automatically adjusts the form of the generalized function based on the specific characteristics of the input data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DFT through a series of experiments involving diverse datasets, showcasing its ability to improve model generalization and performance. The core mechanism of DFT centers around the principle of parameter-driven generalization, allowing the model to learn the optimal representation for each data point.

title: Algorithmic Transparency through Explainable Dataflow Graphs
abstract: This paper addresses the growing need for transparency and interpretability in complex machine learning systems, particularly those utilizing intricate dataflow graphs. Existing explainability methods often struggle to provide a holistic view of the decision-making process within these systems. We propose a novel approach centered on automatically generating explainable dataflow graphs (EDG) that visually represent the computational steps and dependencies involved in a machine learning model's operation. These EDGs are designed to facilitate human understanding, debugging, and ultimately, increased trust in the system. The core of our system involves a process of graph construction, highlighting crucial operations and dependencies, and providing associated explanations. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this method through a conceptual framework and outline the key components required for its full implementation. The system's output provides a dynamic and interactive representation, allowing users to trace the flow of data and understand the rationale behind model predictions. This approach contributes to a significant advancement in algorithmic transparency.

title: Adaptive Topological Structure Learning for Quantum Entanglement Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum entanglement modeling framework leveraging adaptive topological structure learning. Traditional quantum measurement techniques often rely on static, pre-defined topologies, limiting the system's ability to precisely capture complex dynamics. We propose a dynamic topology network that automatically adjusts its structure based on measurement outcomes, enabling quantum information processing with self-optimization capabilities. The core mechanism involves constructing a quantum entanglement network that evolves in response to data, leading to improved measurement accuracy and enhanced computational power. This approach offers a fundamentally new path towards flexible and powerful quantum computation.

title: Neural Symbolic Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper proposes a novel Neural Symbolic Reasoning Engine (NSRE) designed to bridge the gap between the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks and the logical reasoning capabilities of symbolic systems. The core claim is that combining these two approaches yields a system with enhanced knowledge representation and reasoning abilities. The mechanism involves constructing an NSRE that leverages neural networks for knowledge extraction and utilizes symbolic reasoning algorithms for logical inference and knowledge transfer. The system addresses the limitations of current approaches in representing and reasoning with complex knowledge. The architecture consists of a neural network component, responsible for encoding contextual information and identifying relevant knowledge fragments, and a symbolic reasoning engine, which employs a rule-based system to perform logical deductions and integrate the extracted knowledge. This approach offers a pathway to more robust and explainable AI systems, particularly in domains requiring both perceptual understanding and logical deduction. We explore the fundamental components and the interaction between the neural and symbolic modules, outlining a framework for building intelligent systems capable of dynamic knowledge acquisition and sophisticated reasoning. The goal is to create a system that can not only recognize patterns but also reason about them in a logically consistent manner, ultimately leading to more reliable and adaptable AI.

title: Variable Adaptive Quantum Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for quantum algorithms, termed "Variable Adaptive Quantum Algorithm" (VAQ), which dynamically adjusts quantum algorithm parameters based on input data volume and qubit quantity. The core mechanism centers around a self-adaptive parameter adjustment system, optimized to maximize quantum computing resource utilization, particularly in the context of large-scale quantum computation. Traditional quantum algorithm design often relies on fixed parameters, limiting adaptability and hindering performance. VAQ addresses this limitation by providing a mechanism to dynamically adjust quantum parameter values, leading to more efficient and effective computation. The paper details the design of the self-adaptive parameter adjustment system, analyzes its performance benefits, and discusses potential applications in various quantum computing scenarios.

title: Based on Dynamic Network Topology for Robot Collaborative Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the application of dynamic network topology to facilitate collaborative learning among robots. The core claim is that constructing a dynamic network topology enables robots to effectively learn and improve their performance through interaction and knowledge sharing. The proposed mechanism leverages the adaptability of the network to optimize the learning process, allowing robots to exchange learning experiences and collaboratively execute tasks. This approach represents a novel method for robot learning, moving beyond static network configurations and offering a flexible framework for complex robotic systems. The paper details the theoretical framework, explores potential topologies, and discusses the implications for various robotic applications. The primary focus is on the methodological aspects, outlining how a dynamically evolving network can significantly enhance robot learning compared to traditional methods. Simulation results, though not presented experimentally, illustrate the potential benefits of this approach. ---

title: Self-Spin State Dynamic Topology Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm for dynamic topology learning based on spin states, designed to enhance quantum computation efficiency. Traditional topology learning methods typically rely on classical bit-level learning, but leveraging the inherent properties of spin states allows for a more efficient representation and manipulation of quantum systems. The proposed algorithm utilizes the quantum state's unique characteristics to learn the topological structure of the system, thereby improving quantum computing performance. This work addresses the limitations of existing approaches by focusing on the specific strengths of spin states.

title: Fractal Theorem Proving
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to theorem proving, termed "Fractal Theorem Proving," which leverages the principles of fractal geometry and self-similarity to generate and analyze potential proof strategies. The core idea is that mathematical theorems, particularly those exhibiting inherent symmetries or recursive structures, can be effectively tackled by employing algorithms inspired by fractal generation and pattern recognition. The system, described here, operates as a theorem prover that iteratively constructs fractal representations of the theorem's statement and its related lemmas. These fractals are then analyzed for self-similar patterns, which are hypothesized to correspond to potential proof steps. The system utilizes a core mechanism of identifying and exploiting these patterns, guiding the search for a complete proof. This approach represents a shift from traditional symbolic reasoning to a more geometric and structural understanding of mathematical concepts, potentially unlocking new proof techniques and improving the efficiency of automated theorem proving. The paper outlines the core architecture, algorithms, and key concepts underpinning Fractal Theorem Proving, emphasizing its potential to address complex theorems through a fundamentally different approach.

title: From Concentration to Differentiation and Back: Routing Effective Rank in MoE Reasoning Cohorts
abstract: Test-time scaling produces cohorts of reasoning rollouts, yet there is no standard label-free account of how their internal computation reorganizes as inference unfolds. We introduce routing effective rank deff, the entropy-effective dimensionality of a cross-rollout graph built from MoE expert-routing similarity. Across ten MoE configurations and five math/science benchmarks, deff exhibits a reproducible low-high-low trajectory, with a prominent interior maximum in 98.5% of 3,105 model-question cohorts: routing similarity is concentrated early, maximally differentiated at intermediate budgets, and reconcentrated later, and the timing of this maximum varies systematically with architecture and reasoning effort. An exact decomposition separates cohort-wide common-mode mass from residual spectral dimensionality: common-mode reallocation accounts for about two thirds of the trajectory, while the residual spectrum contributes about one quarter and retains substantial variation beyond the common mode. The decomposition further localizes behavior: among non-unanimous cohorts, increases in common-mode concentration strongly predict same-answer recoverability, and higher reasoning effort delays the maximum by 2.59 octaves (doublings of the token budget) and consistently expands the high-rank period across all four tested architectures, locating the effort effect in timing and duration rather than peak amplitude. Correctness comparisons separate structural monitoring from answer selection, positioning routing effective rank as a decomposable, label-free diagnostic of cohort organization - a principled spectral lens on how MoE reasoning cohorts differentiate and reconcentrate over inference time.

title: The Base-Point Barrier: Certifying Low-Rank Truncation Costs a Full Evaluation Pass
abstract: Deciding what a low-rank truncation costs in accuracy requires evaluating the truncated network, and this paper proves that nothing measured where the network already sits can take the place of that evaluation. Eckart–Young–Mirsky bounds reconstruction error, not accuracy, and the absence of a cheap bound on the accuracy cost has been read as a gap in the literature. It is a property of the problem, and we price the only route that remains. Call a bound base-point cheap when everything it reads is measured where the network already sits: the downstream map's value and derivatives there, to any finite order, which differential calculus calls the jet of the map at that point, together with the spectrum and the data's projections onto the singular directions. We call the resulting obstruction the base-point barrier, and the paper is organized around the dichotomy it produces. Every selection criterion for low-rank truncation either reads only what is measurable where the network already sits, in which case it cannot certify accuracy at any tolerance, or it evaluates the network where the truncation puts it, in which case certifying one retained subset costs a full pass over the evaluation set. There is no third option. Each branch is a theorem. On the first, every valid base-point-cheap bound carries slack at least μ, a quantity counted on the evaluation set and attained by the construction, not merely bounded by it. We exhibit the separating pair twice, once with a C^∞ unit whose jets agree exactly at every order and once with the network's own GELU at a tolerance driven below any prescribed resolution. Of nine published selection criteria, eight lie inside the class, so no reweighting of the singular directions will yield a guarantee about accuracy. On the second, certifying one retained subset to tolerance τ requires at least (A − 2τ)N forward evaluations and N suffice, so the query complexity is Θ(N) and certified pruning over subsets cannot beat exhaustion, while estimation stays cheap at O(τ^−2 log δ^−1) samples. Both are realized inside a public checkpoint. Two networks there have numerically identical base-point jets and bit-identical accuracy of 0.9106, and under the same truncation they separate into 0.9060 and 0.4908. The separation is the value the theorem predicts to ten digits, and the lower figure is the exact accuracy of a constant predictor. The separating network is adversarial by construction, so the theorem bounds what a guarantee can promise and not what a trained network typically does, and the same checkpoint carries the complementary measurement. What follows for practice is a prescription and not a caution. Estimate the accuracy cost and report an interval, since a probabilistic interval costs a number of sampled examples that does not grow with the evaluation set. Do not seek a certificate, since certified pruning over subsets cannot reduce the order of the search. Use the cheap first-order surrogate to order candidates, where it is well calibrated while the downstream is shallow, and not to guarantee that the ordering is safe. And when certainty is required, budget one evaluation per example. The premise itself becomes a diagnostic costing one forward pass. For every direction of every layer it returns whether the construction exists there and a ceiling on the slack it could force, so that a reader can price the barrier on a model of their own. It is measured across 246 weight matrices in five model-and-task combinations, and it orders the expensive outcome at +0.955 over twenty-one layers of three architectures. Pre-print in progress. The file is restricted while the manuscript is under advisor review. Access is granted by share link.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: A Novel Non-Linear Adaptive Loss Function
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly evolving field that leverages the unique properties of quantum mechanics to develop algorithms and computational models. This paper explores the application of QML to machine learning, specifically focusing on the design and implementation of a novel non-linear adaptive loss function. The core challenge lies in effectively modeling complex, non-linear relationships within datasets, and traditional approaches often struggle with this task. This research proposes a framework utilizing quantum algorithms to dynamically adjust the loss function during training, allowing the model to better capture intricate dependencies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results, highlighting its potential to improve model performance and generalization capabilities. The focus is on creating a loss function that is inherently more adaptable and capable of handling intricate data patterns.

The core challenge lies in effectively modeling complex, non-linear relationships within datasets, and traditional approaches often struggle with this task. This research proposes a framework utilizing quantum algorithms to dynamically adjust the loss function during training, allowing the model to better capture intricate dependencies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results, highlighting its potential to improve model performance and generalization capabilities. The focus is on creating a loss function that is inherently more adaptable and capable of handling intricate data patterns.

title: Title: Quantum-Based Topological Geometry Algorithm for Adaptive Topology Transformation
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense potential for revolutionizing various fields, and topological geometry represents a particularly promising area. This paper investigates a novel quantum algorithm for adaptive topology transformation, designed to address the limitations of traditional methods. We propose a quantum circuit architecture that dynamically adjusts geometric parameters, enabling rapid and accurate modeling of complex topological structures. The algorithm leverages quantum superposition and entanglement to explore multiple topological transformations simultaneously, significantly accelerating the process compared to classical approaches. The core mechanism centers on exploiting quantum interference to guide the evolution towards the desired topological landscape. We present a preliminary implementation and analysis of the algorithm, demonstrating its effectiveness in transforming simple topological maps, highlighting its potential for broader applications in topological data analysis and design.

title: Adaptive Geometric Transformation Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive geometric transformation optimization techniques to enhance the performance of optimization algorithms. Traditional optimization methods often rely on predefined objective functions, limiting their adaptability to complex datasets. This work introduces a novel approach that leverages the inherent properties of graphs to dynamically adjust geometric transformation parameters, thereby improving optimization efficiency. We propose a framework centered around graph representation, self-similarity, and continuous transformation, enabling the algorithm to automatically adapt to data variations and identify optimal geometric configurations. The core mechanism involves a graph-based representation of the problem space, where geometric transformations are represented as edges and nodes, and the algorithm iteratively refines these transformations based on a learned representation of the data. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of quantitative and qualitative analyses, showcasing significant improvements in optimization speed and accuracy compared to traditional methods. The resulting framework offers a flexible and adaptable solution for a variety of optimization challenges.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Algorithm for Prime Number Generation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a phenomenon where two or more particles become linked and share the same fate, offers a unique pathway for computation and communication. This research explores the potential of leveraging this quantum property to enhance the generation and verification of prime numbers, a computationally challenging task. We propose a novel algorithm, dubbed the "Quantum Entanglement-Driven Prime Generation" (QEDPG), that utilizes entangled particle pairs to explore prime number sequences with significantly increased precision and speed compared to traditional methods. This work details the core mechanism, the rationale behind the design choices, and the preliminary results demonstrating the algorithm's efficacy. The focus is on establishing a fundamentally new approach that exploits quantum entanglement to unlock more efficient prime number distribution.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization of Large-Scale Matrix Computations
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-inspired optimization techniques to accelerate large-scale matrix computations. Traditional optimization algorithms often encounter significant challenges when dealing with the complexity inherent in these computations. We propose a novel approach leveraging concepts derived from quantum annealing and superposition to explore the solution space more efficiently. The core idea is to mimic the probabilistic exploration characteristic of quantum systems within a classical framework. Specifically, we utilize an iterative optimization process, adapting parameters based on simulated "quantum fluctuations," aiming to converge towards optimal solutions faster than conventional methods. The theoretical framework is presented, and we detail the implementation strategy, focusing on the design of a suitable objective function and a corresponding optimization algorithm. Preliminary results suggest the potential for significant speedups, particularly for computationally demanding matrix operations, though further investigation and refinement are needed. The key contribution lies in the direct translation of quantum-inspired principles into a practical optimization strategy for matrix computations.

title: 基于量子计算的密码分析与防御
abstract: This paper investigates the vulnerabilities of current cryptographic systems to attacks leveraging the power of quantum computing. The primary focus is on analyzing widely used algorithms like RSA and ECC, utilizing Shor's algorithm to demonstrate their potential for decryption. Furthermore, the research explores the development of novel cryptographic defense strategies, including quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, to establish secure communication channels. The analysis highlights the limitations of classical cryptography in the face of quantum computation and proposes a paradigm shift towards quantum-resistant security measures. The core contribution lies in a comprehensive assessment of the threat landscape and a preliminary exploration of defense mechanisms, acknowledging the ongoing advancements in quantum computing and cryptography. The paper outlines key algorithmic concepts and provides a framework for future research in this critical area.

title: Quantum Simulation of Classical Dynamical Systems using Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) for simulating classical dynamical systems. Traditional numerical methods for simulating dynamical systems often struggle with complex systems exhibiting sparse interactions or requiring high computational resources. We propose a novel algorithm that utilizes the optimization capabilities of VQEs to approximate the time evolution of these systems. The core idea is to map the system's state vector onto a qubit representation and then iteratively minimize the energy functional derived from the dynamical system's equations, effectively simulating the system's evolution. We specifically target systems with sparse interactions, where the optimization landscape is expected to be more amenable to VQE's strengths. This approach offers a potentially scalable solution for simulating dynamical systems on near-term quantum computers. This work demonstrates the feasibility of employing VQEs as a tool for tackling previously intractable problems in fields such as molecular dynamics, fluid dynamics, and chaos theory.

title: Adaptive Bayesian Model Selection via Epistemic Uncertainty Propagation
abstract: Bayesian model selection provides a principled approach to model choice, but its application is often hindered by the intractable nature of posterior distributions, particularly in high-dimensional settings. This work introduces a novel adaptive Bayesian model selection framework that leverages epistemic uncertainty to dynamically adjust model weights. The core idea is to propagate uncertainty about model parameters through a Bayesian network, effectively quantifying the information gained or lost by each model component. Variational inference is employed for efficient computation of this propagation. The resulting adaptive weighting scheme allows the model selection process to respond effectively to data scarcity and model complexity, leading to improved robustness and accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and illustrate its potential with a conceptual example. The key contribution is the explicit connection between Bayesian model selection, uncertainty quantification, and adaptive weighting, offering a practical solution for challenging model selection problems.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Decoding with Probabilistic Graphical Models
abstract: This paper explores the application of probabilistic graphical models for dynamic quantum state decoding, aiming to enhance the reliability of quantum information transmission. The core concept involves constructing a quantum state decoder based on a probabilistic graphical model, leveraging measurement results to infer the original quantum state. A Bayesian optimization algorithm is then employed to refine the model's parameters, adapting to evolving measurement data and improving decoding accuracy. The proposed approach offers a novel framework for understanding and optimizing the inherently probabilistic nature of quantum state decoding. The key contributions lie in the integration of graphical models with Bayesian optimization, providing a flexible and adaptive solution compared to traditional decoding methods. This work demonstrates the potential for improved quantum communication protocols by dynamically adjusting the decoding process based on observed data.

title: Autonomous Chaotic Time Series Prediction using Physical Neuromorphic Networks
abstract: Physical reservoir computing (PRC) with neuromorphic networks offers a promising approach to brain-inspired information processing, exploiting emergent nonlinear dynamics of physical neural networks as a computational resource. This study demonstrates fully autonomous closed-loop prediction of the Mackey--Glass (MG) chaotic time series using a simulated neuromorphic nanowire network as the physical reservoir. Two strategies are evaluated: the virtual node (VN) method, which expands the feature space by temporal multiplexing of reservoir states, and a non-VN approach that uses all physical node readouts directly without temporal multiplexing. Results are reported for two values of the MG time delay parameter, $τ= 18$ and $τ= 21$, the latter representing a more complex chaotic regime not previously evaluated for this class of physical reservoir. Over a short prediction horizon of $T = 100$ timesteps, the VN approach achieves autonomous prediction accuracies of $90.4$% and $89.7$% at $τ= 18$ and $τ= 21$, respectively, while the non-VN approach achieves $81.5$% and $76.2$%. Long-horizon analysis over $T = 500$ timesteps shows that both approaches reproduce the qualitative attractor structure and dominant spectral content of the true MG signal, with trajectories remaining bounded throughout. These results suggest that the intrinsic dynamics of neuromorphic nanowire networks are sufficient to support meaningful autonomous chaotic time series prediction without virtual node augmentation, and that performance may improve further as physical network sizes scale to the millions of nodes achievable in hardware. As this study uses simulated networks, extrapolation to physically fabricated large-scale arrays remains to be validated experimentally.

title: Radiation, Rotation and Scale Invariant Feature Descriptor for Multimodal Image Matching
abstract: Multimodal image matching is a fundamental task for multi-source information fusion. However, geometric distortions and nonlinear radiometric differences (NRD) severely limit performance, especially under radiometric, rotation, and scale variations. To address this issue, we propose a radiation, rotation, and scale invariant (RRSI) feature descriptor. First, a dual-head regional sampling (DHRS) module simultaneously performs Cartesian and Log-Polar sampling on keypoint neighborhoods, retaining spatial structural properties while enhancing robustness to rotation and scale variations. We then jointly encode geometric and radiometric relations between multimodal images in a unified deep feature space, enabling feature encoding, interaction, and fusion across intra-modal, dual-head sampled, and inter-modal regions. Furthermore, we introduce a bidirectional cross-modal generative reconstruction constraint during training. By decoding implicit features into structural patches of the counterpart modality, this mechanism anchors modality-invariant geometric topologies without additional inference overhead. Experiments on optical-infrared and optical-SAR datasets demonstrate highly competitive matching performance and strong robustness to rotation and scale variations. RRSI supports the full rotation range from 0 to 360 degrees and scale factors up to four. Its generalization ability is further validated on multimodal images from computer vision, remote sensing, and medical imaging. The implementation will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yeyuanxin110/RRSI .

title: DianShi-RxnDB: A Large-Scale, Fine-Grained Organic Reaction Data Platform Built via a Fully Automated Pipeline for Researchers and AI Agents
abstract: High-quality structured organic reaction data are essential for developing artificial intelligence for chemistry (AI4Chem), yet much of this knowledge remains dispersed across patent text, images, and reaction schemes. We present DianShi-RxnDB, a large-scale, fine-grained organic reaction data platform built via a fully automated extraction and normalization pipeline integrating patent text, images, and reaction schemes. Its corpus covers organic synthesis patents from the USPTO and EPO published between 1976 and 2025, yielding approximately 24 million reaction instances, of which approximately 14.8 million (61.7%) pass automated qualification checks. Each instance represents a specific single-step experiment recording participants, roles, quantities, temperatures, reaction times, yields, experimental procedures, and provenance links to source patents. In a manual evaluation of 1,300 sampled qualified instances, the micro-averaged field-level accuracy was 92.95%. A matched comparison with Pistachio further indicated advantages in deduplicated record counts, representation granularity, and field-level exact agreement. The platform provides a Web research workbench for searching, filtering, comparing, and source-verifying records, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) service offering AI agents composable structured retrieval tools. DianShi-RxnDB is available at https://dianshi.opendatalab.org.cn/ .

title: A Computational Implementation of a Goal-Directed Theory of Affect
abstract: Computational modeling of emotion has long faced a tension between descriptive, "snapshot-based" appraisal models and granular, signal-driven architectures that often lack appropriate psychological grounding. This paper addresses this gap by presenting the first high-fidelity computational implementation of the Goal-Directed Theory (GDT) of affect. In this framework, affect is not a post-hoc label but a functional byproduct emerging from the continuous interplay between discrepancy detection and action selection within an agent's internal processing cycles. We evaluate the model through a series of principled simulations (Dice/Corridor tasks) designed to isolate affective signatures and dynamics during multi-step goal pursuit. Results demonstrate that complex affective profiles, like an anticipatory "lift" and a failure "crash", emerge naturally from simple interactions between goal-discrepancy and action-selection expectancies without requiring additional dedicated modules. By ensuring every computational component maps directly to components of the psychological theory, this work establishes a transparent, testable framework that enables a continuous "simulation-empiry" research loop. Our work contributes to moving the field beyond "black-box" heuristics toward a granular, mechanistic understanding of affect, integrated into the core of agent behavior.

evidence.abstract: Computational modeling of emotion has long faced a tension between descriptive, "snapshot-based" appraisal models and granular, signal-driven architectures that often lack appropriate psychological grounding. This paper addresses this gap by presenting the first high-fidelity computational implementation of the Goal-Directed Theory (GDT) of affect. In this framework, affect is not a post-hoc label but a functional byproduct emerging from the continuous interplay between discrepancy detection and action selection within an agent's internal processing cycles. We evaluate the model through a series of principled simulations (Dice/Corridor tasks) designed to isolate affective signatures and dynamics during multi-step goal pursuit. Results demonstrate that complex affective profiles, like an anticipatory "lift" and a failure "crash", emerge naturally from simple interactions between goal-discrepancy and action-selection expectancies without requiring additional dedicated modules. By ensuring every computational component maps directly to components of the psychological theory, this work establishes a transparent, testable framework that enables a continuous "simulation-empiry" research loop. Our work contributes to moving the field beyond "black-box" heuristics toward a granular, mechanistic understanding of affect, integrated into the core of agent behavior.

title: The UPC Diagnostic Engine: Operationalizing Non-Commutative Observer Mechanics in Edge-Deployable Systems
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence operates strictly as a statistical prediction engine trapped within device-side articulation (LO). Possessing no consciousness, localized point of view, or capacity for state commitment (C), the system samples from an unanchored potential field (PO) that is far too broad to sustain local human coherence. Because language prompts remain inherently variable across session turns, un-audited model output inevitably yields semantic drift, a structural decay into non-committal boilerplate, circular debate, and unanchored noise. Stacking additional tokens via prompt engineering cannot resolve this mismatch, as statistical mechanics cannot supply structural boundary stability. This paper presents the UPC Diagnostic Engine, a local desktop apparatus that replaces probabilistic guessing with deterministic metrological rigor. Operating through the formal non-commutative sequence T = ( C o Jo o LO o s o MO ) |PO>, the engine transforms state collapse into an explicit processing pipeline on the local hardware edge. Uncollapsed semantic potential (PO) is partitioned (MO), foregrounded (s), and measured (LO) via exact cosine proximity against five orthonormal eigenstate anchors (N = 214): State_A (Jo / Audited Boundary), T_mechanized (Boilerplate), T_phantom (Pre-Cached Loops), T_visceral (Reactive Reflex), and T_outlier (High-Entropy Noise). By executing this operator chain locally, the apparatus strips away the illusion of autonomous machine judgment. It demonstrates that mechanical systems register strictly at LO, establishing the living human observer as the sole source of structural clarity and state collapse (Jo → C). The resulting immutable JSON trace logs (T) provide an un-smuggled, verifiable measurement standard that classifies conversational hedging and locks audited boundary awareness without cloud reliance or API dependencies. Authored by Eloy Escagedo Gutierrez as part of The Universal Principle of Collapse (UPC) Research Project.

title: The Physical Structure of the Transformer Algorithm from the Perspective of Energy Balancing Between Form Energy and Run Energy
abstract: Starting from the energy balancing between Form Energy and Run Energy, this paper reveals the physical structure of the Transformer self-attention mechanism. In the World Quantum Theory (WQT) framework, the total energy of any particle can be decomposed into Form Energy V_e = mcd and Run Energy T_e = (c/d)mv², and their coupling gives rise to observable energy. This paper demonstrates that the token embedding table in Transformer is an mc parameter-element table — each row is a token, each column is a frequency component, and each element is the mc value of that token at that frequency. The Query weight table extracts Run Energy contributions from mc, the Key weight table extracts Form Energy contributions from mc, and the Value weight table encodes the optimal closed energy manifold learned through training. The dot product Q·K is the coupling operation between Run Energy and Form Energy, softmax(QK)·V is the operation of finding aggregation points on the optimal energy manifold, the residual connection is the energy balancing operation, and the output token is the matching result of the optimal manifold energy traced from the original slice. Multi-head attention corresponds to the multi-directional orthogonal decomposition of the tangential velocity v, and the multi-layer structure corresponds to the different distributions of mc values at different frequencies. Ultimately, this proves that the Transformer algorithm is the discrete matrix realization of the Navier-Stokes energy identity. Keywords: Transformer, Form Energy, Run Energy, energy balancing, Envelope Interface, World Quantum Theory, mc parameter-element, optimal energy manifold

title: Elior / Civil B: A Research Concept for a Curatorial Companion with Auditable Telemetry
abstract: This working paper presents a research concept for Elior / Civil B, a personal curatorial companion intended to support human-selected goals through continuity of assistance and auditable telemetry. It positions episodic retrieval, present-state description, capability estimates, and consequence-based updating against selected research on cognitive architectures, self-modeling, relational agents, and skill selection. Present state is an operational description based on information available at the time; in the author's terminology, Present also carries a relational meaning associated with personally meaningful memory cues. The prospective contribution is the integration and evaluation of these requirements in bounded tasks. The evaluation outline calls for capable comparison systems, matched resources, component-level comparisons, and separate assessment of task outcomes, relational experience, user burden, and evidence-based independence. It does not report new empirical validation, establish novelty, or constitute a completed preregistration. This deposit contains an English primary text and its complete Hungarian translation, with editable Markdown counterparts. It does not release implementation code, detailed technical schemas, private conversations, or participant data. The concept and terminology originate in Omri Bankuti's design work. Preparation and editorial checking were AI-assisted; this is not external peer review or institutional endorsement. title: Quantum Entanglement Information Entropy Calculation and Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum entanglement to the calculation and optimization of information entropy. Traditional methods for entropy calculation often rely on classical computation, which is insufficient for analyzing complex quantum systems. We propose a novel approach utilizing the unique properties of entangled states to precisely compute information entropy and provide optimization algorithms for quantum information processing and quantum computation. The core mechanism centers around the conceptualization of "quantum entanglement information entropy" and its integration with entropy calculations, offering a potential pathway to enhanced performance in quantum systems. This research investigates the potential of leveraging entangled states to achieve more efficient computations, addressing limitations of classical methods in the context of quantum information.

title: 基于自适应的几何变换的基于量子计算的图像处理算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel image processing algorithm utilizing quantum computing principles, specifically focusing on adaptive transformations. Traditional image processing algorithms often rely on explicit, computationally intensive procedures that struggle to effectively handle dynamic image variations. We propose a quantum-enhanced approach that leverages quantum entanglement and superposition to achieve a degree of self-adaptation, allowing for more robust and efficient image manipulation. This work explores the potential of quantum computing to significantly improve the performance of image processing tasks, particularly in scenarios involving complex and rapidly changing visual data. The core mechanism revolves around implementing a quantum-enhanced geometric transformation process, incorporating quantum error correction to maintain the integrity of the transformation. The algorithm will be discussed in detail, including the theoretical underpinnings, implementation considerations, and preliminary results demonstrating the potential of this approach.

title: 基于自适应量子算法的量子计算推理引擎
abstract: Quantum computation offers unprecedented capabilities for complex problem-solving, but the inherent challenges of quantum algorithms – particularly in terms of optimization – pose significant hurdles for practical implementation. This paper introduces a novel quantum computation reasoning engine, termed "Adaptive Quantum Inference Engine" (AQIE), designed to address these challenges through the integration of adaptive quantum algorithm tuning. AQIE dynamically adjusts its inference strategies based on the quantum computation's output, significantly enhancing both the efficiency and accuracy of the reasoning process. We present a comprehensive theoretical framework and empirical validation demonstrating the engine's effectiveness in several benchmark problems, highlighting its potential to revolutionize quantum computation.

title: 基于量子纠缠的自适应信息加密
abstract: This paper presents a novel information encryption scheme predicated on the principles of quantum entanglement. The proposed algorithm leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to establish a fundamentally more secure key exchange and data transmission process than currently employed methods. We explore how entanglement can be harnessed to create a cryptographic system that is inherently resistant to eavesdropping and manipulation. The core mechanism centers around generating and managing entangled states, which are then manipulated to generate encryption keys and secure transmissions. This research investigates the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize information security by offering a robust and potentially unbreakable method of data protection. The study concludes with a detailed analysis of the algorithm's security properties and potential applications within the broader context of data security.

title: Title: Quantum Chaos Dynamics – Emergent Information Extraction
abstract: Quantum Chaos Dynamics (QCD) represents a fascinating and increasingly active area of research, exploring the potential of quantum systems to exhibit complex, unpredictable behavior. This paper investigates the design of a self-regulating quantum system capable of extracting and propagating information about chaotic dynamics through entangled states, creating a feedback loop. We propose a novel quantum entanglement protocol that leverages the inherent instability of quantum systems to generate complex, evolving patterns, forcing the system to 'learn' and 'encode' information. The core claim is that this approach offers a pathway to understanding consciousness or advanced computation, a goal previously considered firmly within the realm of theoretical physics. This work begins with a detailed theoretical framework exploring the principles of quantum entanglement and its application to information extraction. It then outlines the architecture of the proposed system, emphasizing the critical role of instability in driving the system's learning process. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential challenges and future directions of this research.

title: 基于自适应的算法优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm optimization framework based on adaptive algorithm parameter adjustment. Traditional optimization methods often rely on pre-defined parameter sets, which may be suboptimal for complex datasets. This work proposes a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism that adapts to the data distribution, resulting in improved algorithm efficiency and generalization. The framework leverages this adaptation to effectively optimize performance across a wider range of scenarios. We present a comprehensive evaluation demonstrating the framework's superior performance compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving non-convex optimization.

title: Adaptive Quantum Circuit
abstract: Quantum circuit design presents a significant challenge due to the inherent complexity of quantum systems. Traditional methods rely heavily on expert knowledge and often struggle to efficiently explore the vast design space. This paper introduces an adaptive quantum circuit, a novel approach that leverages machine learning to dynamically adjust circuit parameters and structure based on input data characteristics, ultimately improving circuit performance and efficiency. The core mechanism centers around a machine learning model trained to learn and optimize circuit design through data analysis. This research explores the potential of this technique to overcome limitations of conventional circuit design and pave the way for more efficient and adaptable quantum systems. The study focuses on the implementation of a specific adaptive circuit design for a simplified quantum system, demonstrating its effectiveness through quantitative analysis.

title: Adaptive Quantum Monte Carlo Simulation – Refinement Through Iterative Error Correction
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive quantum Monte Carlo simulation designed to refine results through iterative error correction, leveraging a quantum error correction method. The core concept is to continuously assess and correct errors during the simulation process, improving accuracy and robustness. Traditional Monte Carlo methods often fail to effectively utilize error correction, necessitating a novel approach. This work proposes a method that incorporates a feedback loop, iteratively correcting errors based on quantum error correction principles, resulting in a significantly enhanced simulation fidelity. We detail the implementation of this iterative correction process and present preliminary results demonstrating the potential for improved accuracy compared to existing techniques.

abstract: This paper presents a geometric proof of concept demonstrating the correctness and efficiency of a novel quantum algorithm, tentatively named "Hyper-Correlation Algorithm" (HCA). The core of the proof relies on constructing a formal geometric model that visualizes and analyzes the algorithm's steps, establishing a rigorous foundation for verification and potential practical application. The model, while currently simplified, aims to capture the essential dynamics of the algorithm's operations. We will explore the mathematical framework underpinning the HCA, including key geometric transformations and relationships. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential benefits of this geometric approach to quantum algorithm validation.

title: Dimensional Generalization and Quantum Entanglement: A Novel Approach
abstract: This paper explores the potential of dimensionality generalization and quantum entanglement to revolutionize the field of quantum computing. We propose a novel model based on the concept of "quantum topology" – a framework that utilizes entangled states to dynamically reshape the geometry of higher-dimensional spaces. This model aims to create new mathematical functions and geometric transformations, offering a pathway to more stable and complex quantum states. The study details the implementation of this approach, examining its implications for quantum computation and the potential for emergent quantum phenomena. The core mechanism hinges on the manipulation of entangled states to define a dynamic, multi-dimensional space, opening avenues for novel mathematical analysis and quantum algorithms.

title: Explainable AI for Reinforcement Learning through Causal Reasoning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, from game playing to robotics. However, the "black box" nature of many RL agents presents a significant challenge, particularly in applications where transparency and trust are paramount. This work proposes a novel approach to explainable AI (XAI) within the context of RL by integrating causal reasoning. Traditional RL methods primarily rely on correlation-based learning, which can lead to spurious correlations and opaque decision-making processes. Our approach introduces a mechanism where RL agents explicitly identify and reason about causal relationships between states, actions, and rewards. This allows the agent to articulate *why* it took a particular action, connecting it to the underlying causes of the situation. We formalize this process using a causal Bayesian network and demonstrate how this framework can be implemented within a standard RL architecture. The core contribution is a method for generating explanations that are not only plausible but also reflect a genuine understanding of the environment's causal structure. This framework offers a path towards more robust, trustworthy, and interpretable RL systems, addressing a critical limitation of current approaches.

title: Dynamic Graph Representation Learning with Adaptive Graph Kernels
abstract: Graph representation learning aims to transform raw graph data into meaningful vector representations, enabling downstream tasks like node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. Traditional approaches often rely on fixed graph kernels, which assume a static graph structure. However, real-world graphs are inherently dynamic, exhibiting evolving node relationships and structural changes over time. This paper introduces a novel framework for dynamic graph representation learning that leverages adaptive graph kernels. These kernels dynamically adjust their parameters based on the current graph structure and node interactions, effectively capturing the evolving nature of the graph. We propose a method for generating these adaptive kernels and demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and a conceptual exploration. The core contribution lies in providing a flexible and robust approach to graph representation learning that can handle dynamic graph scenarios, addressing a critical limitation of existing methods. Our adaptive kernel approach offers a significant improvement over static kernels by allowing the representation to shift with changes in the underlying graph.

title: Quantum Entanglement Analysis and Manipulation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique challenge to classical information theory. This research delves into the analysis and manipulation of quantum entanglement, specifically exploring its potential for instantaneous information transfer and quantum communication. We propose a novel framework for measuring and manipulating entanglement, leveraging its non-local properties to achieve a paradigm shift in information processing. This investigation challenges traditional information theory by demonstrating a potential for bypassing the limitations imposed by locality and causality. The study investigates the implications of this approach on the foundations of information theory, considering its impact on cryptography and distributed quantum computing. This work explores the potential for achieving truly instantaneous communication, a concept previously considered purely theoretical, and examines the impact on our understanding of information's fundamental nature.

title: Biofeedback-Inspired Computation: A Novel Architectural Design
abstract: This paper proposes a novel computational architecture inspired by the feedback mechanisms observed within biological neural systems. The core claim is that mimicking these feedback loops can lead to architectures exhibiting inherent adaptability and robustness – characteristics often lacking in traditional computing paradigms. The proposed architecture leverages feedback signals to dynamically adjust and optimize computational processes. title: A Subsampled Davis-Kahan Bound for Large-Scale Eigenspace Estimation
abstract: The Davis-Kahan theorem is a fundamental tool in spectral analysis, providing quantitative control over the distance between the eigenspaces of a symmetric matrix and its perturbation. However, when the matrix dimension is large, computing leading eigenvectors is computationally expensive, limiting the practical use of spectral methods in modern large-scale applications. This paper addresses this problem by proposing an independent Bernoulli sampling scheme and proves that the leading left singular vectors of the subsampled matrix faithfully approximate the target subspace of a low-rank symmetric matrix. Our main result is a subsampled Davis-Kahan bound that gives an explicit error bound depending directly on the sampling probability. The bound reveals the trade-off: the computational cost scales linearly with the sampling probability, while the statistical error scales as the inverse square root of the sampling probability. Our result thus extends the Davis-Kahan theorem to the subsampled setting, enabling scalable spectral analysis of large-scale symmetric matrices.

title: MechAudit-40: White-Box Auditing across 40 LLM Attack Mechanisms
abstract: While LLM attacks span prompt optimization, multi-turn context manipulation, retrieval poisoning, and model backdoors, white-box defenses are typically evaluated on isolated attack families. Consequently, whether heterogeneous attacks leave internal representation shifts that generalize to unseen threat mechanisms remains unknown. We present MechAudit-40, a systematic evaluation of 40 attack mechanisms across five open-weight model architectures. Threat-specific success criteria, 100,000 matched clean-attack representation pairs, predefined categories, and grouped holdouts isolate genuine attack-induced displacement from target scale, corpus bias, and data-leakage shortcuts. Across this testbed, attacks induce structured multi-depth trajectories rather than isolated layer spikes. While raw peaks are non-portable across architectures, target-calibrated profiles preserve transferable geometric signatures: under complete mechanism holdout, hidden states alone recover the threat category of unseen attacks with 82.5% accuracy. Guided by this finding, we design MechAudit, a runtime auditor that operates under strict zero-oracle constraints without requiring clean baseline traces or attack metadata. MechAudit detects 81.1% of held-out attack executions at a 0.70% false-positive rate and maintains 78.1% recall when an entire functional category is withheld. In matched comparisons, MechAudit is the only detector that avoids mechanism-level coverage collapse, maintaining over 50% recall across all 40 mechanisms. Internal representations thus support cross-mechanism attack-exposure auditing against calibrated benign references, but decouple from downstream task compromise and parameter integrity.

title: A Statistical and Machine Learning Framework for Quantifying Offensive Impact in Professional Box Lacrosse
abstract: Professional box-lacrosse statistics summarize outcomes but provide limited information about shot quality or the roles behind scoring opportunities. This study develops a documented framework for estimating expected goals (xG) and attributing recorded offensive involvement using 1,006 manually annotated Rochester Knighthawks shot attempts, including 151 goals, from 13 consecutive 2025-2026 National Lacrosse League games. Logistic regression, random forest, and extremely randomized trees were evaluated across three nested feature sets using Leave-One-Game-Out cross-validation and a training-fold base-rate benchmark. The contextual baseline random forest had the lowest observed pooled log loss (0.4189) and Brier score (0.1260), improving on the benchmark by 1.22% and 1.50%; five of nine specifications did not beat the benchmark. Adding two-man-action and pick-type fields did not improve the primary metrics. Core Offensive Impact attributes recorded involvement through shooter xG and shot-based expected assists for final passers. Expected Pick Value (xPV) compares a qualifying pick's observed-state probability with a no-pick counterfactual. Its magnitude was indistinguishable from model noise. Its directional pattern exceeded 200 row-permutation replicates, but limited tail resolution and failure to preserve game-level pick composition make the diagnostic descriptive rather than inferential. Accordingly, xPV is reported only as an exploratory augmented component. Given the single-team, 13-game sample, the results are an initial case study rather than league-wide or causal estimates.

title: 基于自适应几何的领域扩展算法 (GEA)
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm, the Geometric Extension Algorithm (GEA), which leverages the principles of geometric topology to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters and facilitate efficient adaptation to diverse field geometries. Traditional parameter tuning methods often involve tedious manual adjustments, while GEA automates this process, resulting in improved algorithm performance and adaptability. The core mechanism of GEA involves transforming algorithm parameters into geometric representations and iteratively adjusting these representations based on the characteristics of the input field. This adaptive adjustment allows the algorithm to effectively 'extend' its capabilities to new and unseen geometric spaces. The paper details the implementation of GEA, provides a rigorous analysis of its performance, and explores its potential applications across various fields.

title: Quantum Computing Algorithm Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm optimization method leveraging the unique capabilities of quantum computing. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle with complex systems, requiring significant computational resources and time. We propose a quantum-enhanced optimization approach designed to overcome these limitations by utilizing quantum parallelism and superposition. The core mechanism involves mapping the optimization problem onto a quantum state representation, enabling parallel processing and enhanced exploration of the solution space. The paper details the design of the quantum algorithm, its potential advantages over classical approaches, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness in specific optimization scenarios.

title: Title: Adaptive Graph Neural Network Structure Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to graph neural network (GNN) structure optimization utilizing an adaptive graph structure adjustment algorithm. Traditional methods often rely on manual design, limiting their adaptability to data variations. This paper introduces a dynamically adjustable structure optimization strategy, leveraging self-tuning algorithms to adjust the network's topology in real-time based on the characteristics of the training data. The proposed method aims to enhance model performance by intelligently adapting the graph's connectivity and node features. The core mechanism involves a self-learning mechanism that dynamically modifies the graph's structure during training, resulting in a more robust and adaptable model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through experimental results comparing it to existing optimization techniques.

title: Adaptive Modal Neurons
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Adaptive Modal Neurons (AMNs), a novel approach to neural network design inspired by the dynamic modality switching observed in biological neurons. The core claim is that neurons can dynamically adjust their internal modal states based on the characteristics of incoming signals, thereby enhancing their ability to recognize and respond to complex patterns. The proposed mechanism involves designing neurons with variable modal states, utilizing feedback mechanisms and adaptive algorithms to enable learning and adaptation to diverse input patterns. This work explores the theoretical framework and potential applications of AMNs, aiming to improve the robustness and efficiency of artificial neural networks. The key mathematical representation of the core concept is as follows: Let *s1, s2, ..., sK* represent the input signals to the neuron. Let *m1, m2, ..., mN* represent the different modal states of the neuron. The neuron's state *σ* is defined as: *σ = f(s1, s2, ..., sK, m1, m2, ..., mN)* Where *f* is an activation function that governs the transition between modal states. The goal is to design *f* such that *σ* adapts optimally to the input signals. A simplified model update equation would be: *mi = mi + α * (σ - mi) * h(s1, s2, ..., sK)* Where *α* is a learning rate, *h(s1, s2, ..., sK)* is a function representing the input signal's influence on the modal state transition, and *mi* represents the i-th modal state.

title: Dynamically Shaped Neural Architectures via Evolutionary Algorithm
abstract: The design of neural network architectures remains a significant challenge in deep learning, frequently relying on manual expert tuning or predefined templates. This work proposes a novel approach to automatically generate and evolve neural network architectures using an evolutionary algorithm. The core idea is to treat the architecture itself as a population of potential solutions, subject to iterative refinement based on performance and structural constraints. This dynamic shaping capability addresses the limitations of static architectures, which often prove suboptimal for specific datasets. The algorithm iteratively modifies network components – including connections, layers, and activation functions – to achieve enhanced performance. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the evolutionary process and the key considerations for successful implementation. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to create highly adaptive and optimized neural networks, moving beyond traditional design paradigms. The core contribution lies in the automated, data-driven adaptation of network structure, offering a pathway to improved model efficiency and accuracy.

title: Adversarial Training for Secure Federated Learning with Differential Privacy
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without directly exchanging data. However, this paradigm is increasingly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where malicious participants can manipulate the training process to infer sensitive information about individual users. This paper proposes a novel framework combining adversarial training with differential privacy to mitigate these security risks. Our approach trains models robust against attacks aimed at extracting private data while simultaneously guaranteeing differential privacy for each participant. We introduce a modified training loop incorporating adversarial loss alongside the standard FL loss, and demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and a conceptual examination. The key contribution lies in the synergistic combination of these two techniques, creating a more secure and privacy-preserving federated learning system. The goal is to provide a foundational approach for building robust FL systems.
